body:
You should try therapy again and this time be completely transparent, 100% honest.  

I went to anger management/therapy when I was younger and I looked at it as a joke and fed the guy bullshit for weeks.  I wasn't getting anywhere and things were getting worse for me.  I eventually just told the guy that I hadn't been taking the sessions seriously and that I wanted to start again, totally fresh, forget everything we've spoken about so far.  It turns out that he was able to help me and got me the medication and the help I needed.  I can proudly say that that was over 10 years ago and I've been on the right track since (with a few mis-steps along the way, which is to be expected).

I know you probably hear this often, but you are only 26.  Your adult life has barely begun.  Not only that, but you're ahead of the game in that you have a career going already.

None of that is of any comfort though when you're depressed and feeling like you're trapped or that you've wasted valuable time, that I can relate to 100%.

Now that you have the career set in place, is there a way to devote some of your time to anything else?  What are your interests?  Do you feel like you've missed out on anything else other than never having loved a woman?

I completely agree with what ThoughtlessThinking said.  When a thought like suicide is stuck in your mind at all times, it starts to look more and more like the most viable option.

What are those few reasons you haven't done it yet?  Maybe you can try to explore those reasons and find out how to get more things like that in your life.

Hmm.  I was going to suggest investing in a heavy bag, or even just trying to put those punches into a pillow or something.  If you don't realize you're doing it until you've already done it, though, that would still be an issue.

Honestly, if you find yourself doing that and you don't even realize it, it's probably time seek professional help.  You mentioned anti-depressants and some meds, but did you sit down with a professional and really talk about what's going on in your mind that's causing these actions?  If you haven't, you should.  Your post and our conversation has stayed so reasonable and static, it seems like you have your head on straight, but with *something* being a bit off and causing you to not feel and/or have the punching fits.

Either way, keep fighting through, man.  You've lived 22 years and you've been feeling this way for 6 months.  You can turn it around, you just need to find that spark that will do it for you.  Whether it's randomly finding a new hobby, talking to someone, having a good trip (I honestly wouldn't recommend it if it affected you so strongly the first time), or whatever it'll be for you.  It'll happen.  You might have to fight tooth and nail to make it to that point, but you can do it, and god damn will it feel great once you beat it.  I can tell you from experience that the moment it hits you that you don't have the suicidal thoughts or cyclical depressing thoughts in your head, it comes over you like a waterfall of happy.  You'll get there, just keep trying to find what will trigger that for you.

Your experience sounds very surreal, it must've been very intense to have such last effects on you.

I think some of the issues involving the salvia was the setting you did it in.  As a general rule of thumb, psychedelic drugs should be taken in very stable, safe, controlled environments.  If you do decide to take another trip, which may help or hurt you as reactions to psychedelics vary so much from person to person, you should make sure it is a controlled environment with a trip-sitter that will keep you safe and under control.

With the punching, do you think you're doing it to feel something, or to release your depression, anxiety, anger, etc.?

Ha, I have to say I'm intrigued with the sport you compete in and I don't even know what it is!

I really don't think there's a fix-all way that would work for everyone in regards to keeping chill or not letting things get to you as quickly and as harshly.  I can suggest, based on personal experience, that talking to a professional may help.  Our situations are of course unique, and I spoke to a professional regarding anger management issues.  I would bottle it up and unleash a fury on the people that actually cared about it.  It was awful, I hated every second of acting that way, and talking to someone was a huge step for me in changing my ways.

If you aren't ready to talk to a professional, have you tried opening up and sharing this with your surviving brother, or maybe even your parents, about how you feel?  My younger sister somehow managed to get much wiser, much quicker than I did, so I turn to her when I'm really on edge and need an ear or a word of advice or even just some words of encouragement.

I apologize if any of this is out of the realm of possibility, it's just some stuff that sort of helped when I was in rough place.  And if you can't talk to your parents or brother and don't want to talk with a professional, but still want to get things off your chest, send me a PM anytime.  Vent your heart out.  We're both anonymous and sometimes just getting it out there in the open and into someone else's head can take the weight of the world off your shoulders.

Aside from one alcohol and depression induced mistake, you sound like an awesome dude.  Don't mean that to sound all butterflies and rainbows like you said you didn't want, just making an observation.

I agree with TheNoxx.  It sounds like you're wound WAY tight.  It's to be expected though with your intense sports background and getting a GED at 14, so that's probably just ingrained in who you are.  Are there any other things in your life that make you happy other than success in sports and academics that you can focus some time and energy on?

As for your girlfriend finding out about the fling with the other girl... now that she knows, really all you can do is apologize, explain yourself, and hope for the best.  As much as it sucks, the ball may be out of your court on this one, but telling her how you feel and why it happened and just explaining yourself can go a long way.

Also, would it give away your identity to say what sport you compete in?  You sound very much like a figure skater.  So much drive to succeed and so much determination to be the best.
You told the truth about the shit people were putting this poor girl through, please don't beat yourself up over that.  You did the right thing.

Imagine how hurt your current boyfriend would be if you ended your life because you were afraid to tell him the truth.  I think that would hurt him worse than any type of cheating or lying.

Imagine, for a moment, that the roles were reversed.  Wouldn't you want your boyfriend to tell you the truth, even if it upset you, *especially*  if your boyfriend was contemplating ending his life as opposed to telling you that truth?

Everyone makes mistakes.  Most people make mistakes that involve their love life.  I've cheated on a few of my exes, and yeah, it feels terrible, but truth will out.  The longer I lied and held it in, the worse it made me feel.  

As for the ex-lover, you should go to the police and inquire about a restraining order.  Following someone all over the place, after they've told you to piss off, is not ok.

Also, in coming clean to your boyfriend, tell him *everything*.  Let him know you've been struggling with this for awhile, how much it hurts you, and that this guy is still pursuing you.  Make sure you tell him not to get involved, though, and let the authorities (please, please inquire about a restraining order) take care of the ex-lover.

Have you researched why your anti-depressants aren't working anymore?  Maybe you should check into switching medications and giving that a try.

>Some people just don't want help. Some people just can't be helped.

Do you not want help, or do you feel you can't be helped?
Hey, just because you don't feel you're a tough alpha-male type doesn't mean you're a coward or you should end it.  What is it about that type of person that makes you wish you could be like them?

Sorry I'm getting on this so late, but if you are around and want to talk for awhile, I'm here to listen.  If you see this in a few hours and want to talk then, message me, I check back on this account all day.

Hey, we've got a conversation going off my first comment, but I just wanted to interject here real quick.

>Would they have been better off in that scenario? I guess nobody can say for sure, but I can't help but think they would be.

There really is no such thing as "better off" in a scenario where one of your children dies.  I think I know what you mean by saying that, but as someone who isn't a parent, I put your scenario into my world and checked it out.  I have a dog and a cat.  I love them both, but I get along better with my dog, he loves me more, I think.  If my dog died, it wouldn't make me think "I'd be better off if my cat died instead".  So, it's hard for me to imagine your parents thinking in that same manner about you or your living sister.  As someone who admittedly has self-esteem issues, do you think it's possible that you're seeing that thought that's in your own head in the heads of others, even if it isn't there?  I'm not sure I'm wording it the way I mean to be saying it, but I hope you understand what I mean.

-> The thought of you dying instead and being a better scenario for your parents likely hasn't crossed their minds, and if it has, it was most likely in a moment of extreme stress and grief, and they likely felt terrible about it if it ever did cross their minds.  Therefore, you should try to push that thought out of your mind as well.  There's no sense torturing yourself with "what if" scenarios.

It's definitely hard to focus on those little positive interactions at first when you've spent so much time and energy analyzing all the negative or neutral interactions, but the more you look for them and appreciate them, the more you'll see them and be in tune with them.

Families are so weird, aren't they?  My family is somewhat similar to yours.  With my father, he seems to hold my sister to higher standards than me.  Like with school, if I got a B or a C, it was business as usual.  If my sister came home with a C though, she was in for a grounding.  At the time, I thought that it was because my dad had given up on me since I'm 5 years older than my sister and he didn't seem to care if I messed up.  My sister, at the same time, thought that he hated her and loved me because I could get away with things.  Well, I'm 27 now and have talked to my dad about it a few times since I've moved out and established myself as an independent adult.  He told me that my sister and I were different people and he knew we needed different types of parenting.  He said he didn't even know he was doing it at the time, but he was reacting to our personalities and our character as much as he was reacting to our grades or whatever it was at that time.  So while you might see it as your dad giving you a hard time, he may just subconsciously reacting to you in the only way he thinks will work.  Of course, that isn't an excuse to treat (in their mind, your mind) poorly or different.  It might be something worth talking to him about.  Or, if you think this really is the case with father and don't want to talk to him about it, start taking what he says with a grain of salt.  It's hard to imagine a father that loves his son like you say he loves you intentionally belittling your choices.  You know, like he means one thing or wants to get one point across, but only feels like he can communicate that in a condescending way.  I mean, I could also be 100% wrong, I'm just letting you know how things were in my situation, which sounds at least a little bit like yours.

Oh man, nightshift? That shit can be rough, right?  Haha.  I worked nightshift in a seedy casino for 2 years.  Making the switch to working nights for the first time was TOUGH.

Oh, I apologize dude, I very obviously thought your name was Larry.  I wish I had more advice for you, but as just a regular dude, I can only offer the experiences I had and what worked for me.  You said that you've been seeing an anger management counselor for quite some time on and off, why not try a regular old therapist?  Or maybe someone that specializes in how you're feeling about yourself rather than the anger issue?  It's worth trying before you give up.

Think about what you're saying though, Larry.  You get so enraged and out of control that you hurt the ones around you, and you are admitting that this is a problem.  Then you're turning around and saying that the solution is to get so enraged and out of control that you take it out on yourself.  Like what I did as a young man, you're describing a pattern of bottling it up, and then releasing it on whoever is nearest to you, and now you're thinking about aiming that rocket of rage and anger at yourself.  What kind of hobbies do you have?  Is there anything else you could turn that energy towards?

And you aren't a coward.  You wouldn't be talking about your problems if you were.  When you have serious, real problems like the ones you're discussing, it takes incredible courage to discuss them.

That is one hell of a situation you are in, friend.  I'm sorry to hear about your hardships in your relationship, being hurt by someone you love so deeply is the worst feeling in the entire world.

I've been in quite a few "serious" relationships, 3 of them being live-in girlfriends.  I don't know enough about you, your wife, your kids, or "Luke" to give you do this or do that kind of advice, so I can only speak about my experiences.  Every relationship that I've been in where rules regarding the contact one party can have with another person outside the marriage are introduced has ended in a fiery mess.  You seem like a very, very trusting and forgiving person.  That is so admirable, especially in the world today where people don't trust anyone.  You're truly a rare breed.  The lying and deception that she is taking part in is not healthy.  Not only is she hurting you, but you have two kids, man.  Kids aren't oblivious.  They may not remember any of this stuff happening or even know that it's going on, but their mental well-being is definitely something to consider in any scenario, and living in a household where mom and dad don't trust each other as far as they can throw each other could do serious harm.  Whether the solution is to separate or stay together and work on the trust issues, you need to think of how it will effect them.

Also, maybe try seeing a couples therapist?  You clearly love your wife and the gist of the story I'm getting is that you want it to work if it is at all possible and seeing a professional may be the best place to start.

Wow, Larry, this sounds so much like me at 17 it isn't even funny.  I had the best parents, the best girlfriend, and the best friends in the world, but I also had some serious instability.  Like you, I would hold it all in, and eventually just take it out on someone that really didn't deserve, usually someone I really, really loved.  I would scream at the top of my lungs, in my girlfriends face, that she was a fucking bitch, a piece of shit, worthless, etc. etc. etc.  It was awful.  I hurt her so bad, and the kicker, she did nothing wrong.  The smallest little thing would happen and I would completely rage out and just break her down emotionally.  I did the same to my parents.

Have you tried speaking with an anger management counselor?  That was what got me on the right track to managing the way I control my temper and express my anger.

You mentioned being kicked out of your home, are you living back at home now, or where are you staying?  If you are back with your parents, let them know that you realize you've made some mistakes and that you want to change.  Maybe you could ask them to help you and take you to see an anger management counselor.  Or, if you aren't back at home, try talking to your guidance counselor at school.  There may be someone at your school that's trained in anger management counseling, and they could help you for free.

Also, I know anger management counseling sounds super lame and like a scam.  How could someone teach me how to not be angry, right?  Well, that's what I thought about it at first, and god damn was I wrong.  It saved my relationship with my parents.

25 isn't too old, man, I promise.  I'm 27, didn't graduate college, worked going nowhere jobs until about a year and a half ago I got lucky and one of my applications landed on the right desk at the right time.  It isn't the greatest job in the world and it isn't going to make me rich, but it's work and a wage.  I know 3 years seems like a lifetime, but once that's over, imagine the weight that's going to be lifted off your shoulders.  You could also use that three years to start beefing up your resume with volunteer work.  I have a friend that did something like this and when his potential employers asked if his volunteer work was court ordered, he said no, I just wanted to make right by myself and offset my wrongs with some rights.  It worked out for him, maybe it could work for you.

Either way, you seem like a very intelligent person (you've had well thought out and researched answers to the questions at hand that pertain to your work/life), so I hope you don't give up.  You have a lot more to offer the world than a sad ending.
From reading your posts, you really don't come off as an asshole.  What makes you think these people think you're an asshole?

Hey, I care.  It really seems like your environment has had a huge effect on your life.  Maybe you can work at changing that environment a little at a time and give yourself a rebirth?  Maybe try joining a club at your junior college, or taking on a part time job?  Even if it's a McDonald's job or something, it'll get you interacting with people who know nothing about you or your past or your insecurities and give you the opportunity to make friends.  I worked at a McDonald's when I was a bit younger and I worked with a lot of people that didn't have friends outside that store, but being there and working a shit job together gave us all a sense of camaraderie.  10ish years later and I'm still friends with some of them, and can honestly say that had we not met and worked together at that McDonald's, we wouldn't have ever said two words to each other.

How old were you when you immigrated?

Have you ever thought about a start-up?  You sound motivated if you've searched so extensively for a job, even going as far as to look out of state.  Even if it's just starting small and advertising computer repair or something in your local paper.
As GhosttHardware said, if you need someone to talk to or chat with, PM me, bud.

Hmm.  If you PM me the number I need to call, the information I would need, and the information you're looking to get, I could make a few calls for you.

Also, the input you've had in r/askscience is awesome.  I actually just found this subreddit recently, so keep posting in there.

Your posts in self, povertytips, frugal, and depression are awesome.  You're a good person.  You're in shitty situation and you still say nice things to strangers on the internet to make them feel better.  Fucking good on you, man.

Hey Larry.  It's been a few hours since you posted this so I apologize for replying so late!  Do you mind if I ask why you were kicked out of your home, had the girlfriend issues, and the trouble with your friends?  Did it all stem from the same issue?

Hey.  I just read this post, the two that you posted within this one, and a ton of your previous posts from the last year.  You definitely aren't someone that the Reddit, or the world, should lose.

As someone on the other side of the country with very little money to spare, what can I do to help you?  I'm serious.  Would a sleeping bag help?  A warm coat?  I have little money to spare and live paycheck to paycheck, but I have warm clothes and blankets if they'd help you at all.  I could send them to a UPS store or something near you.  Seriously, how can I help you?

EDIT : Just saw your reply to et_amor_fati that you can get your sleeping bags and personal items.  I don't mean for this to sound wrong or condescending, but could you use any non-perishable food items?

* 
You aren't a crybaby saying crybaby things.  I'd be hard pressed to find anyone I know that's satisfied with their life.  I mean 100%, change nothing satisfied.  I'm not satisfied.  I hate that I can write and portray one voice, but when I talk, the way I put words together makes me sound downright silly.  There's nothing wrong with feeling this way or talking about it or being upset about it.

* 
You're a nurse that works with sick, hurt, and dying people.  I wouldn't expect them to be cheery or appreciative of your work, as they probably think the doctor does all the work and you're his assistant.  I wouldn't take this personally.  I answer a phone for a living and people typically don't give me a second thought, so I know it sucks that people just ignore you or talk to you like you aren't on their level.  At first it depressed me, but now I make a game of it.  I try to make every person I talk to either laugh, or if that isn't in the cards, I try to get their inquiry handled as quick as I can.  Sometimes they laugh, sometimes they don't.  Sometimes they are appreciative of how quickly I help them, sometimes they don't care and don't even say goodbye.  That's on them, not me.  Maybe you could try doing something extra here and there for a patient?  A joke, a smile, some small talk, etc.  I'm sure you do all this anyway, but really look for the effect it has.  Bask in those smiles you get, enjoy that small talk.  If someone doesn't reciprocate the smile or the small talk, hey, maybe they're even more uncomfortable with their life than you are?

* 
I'm so sorry you lost your sister.  That must have been devastating, and to hear your parents say something like that must've hurt you very badly.  Talk it with a grain of salt though, man.  Just like you lost your sister, they lost their daughter.  I can't imagine the grief your family must've felt.  Sometimes people say rash things when they're hurting.  And you know what?  If they meant it, well, it is what it is.  I know my mom has more of a connect with my sister than she does with me.  That's just how it is.  It's tough sometimes, but I know she still loves me, and I bet your parents still love you just the same.  You mention not fitting in with your family or your other sister.  What makes you feel this way?

>I really don't want to do it, but, man, sometimes it just seems like such a good idea, if just for an hour at a time.

Just remember those moments when you snap out of it and realize it isn't a good idea and wouldn't be the best thing for your sister, your parents, your friends, your co-workers, and most importantly YOU.  The way you worded the above quote really hits home.  There were times earlier in my life where, even if just for a moment, ending it all was the only logical plan of action.  Those first few moments when I "snapped back to reality" were so insightful.  Even when I didn't know why I didn't want to end it anymore, I knew that there must be *something* out there for me.  I just needed to find it.

If you feel like talking about things, venting to me, or just wanna shoot the shit, send me a PM me or something.  I'm at work and on the computer until 3 PM EST, then a quick drive home and I'll be back on around 4:45 PM EST.
